The Gītā-dhyānam — the meditation verses traditionally chanted before the Bhagavad Gītā. They salute the Gītā as the mother who showers the nectar of non-duality, Vyāsa the compiler, and Kṛṣṇa the teacher; picture the Upaniṣads as cows milked by the cowherd for Arjuna the calf; and describe the Kurukṣetra war as a river crossed with Keśava as the ferryman.

Chapter 1 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Arjuna-viṣāda-yoga (the Yoga of Arjuna's Despondency). On the field of Kurukṣetra, Sañjaya describes to the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra the two armies arrayed for battle and the blowing of the conches. Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to draw his chariot between the armies, sees his teachers, kinsmen and friends on both sides, and overcome by grief and confusion, lays down his bow, refusing to fight.

Chapter 2 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Sāṅkhya-yoga (the Yoga of Knowledge). Arjuna surrenders to Kṛṣṇa as a disciple, and the teaching begins: the Self is never born and never dies, and is not slain when the body is slain; one's own duty (svadharma) is to be done; action is to be performed without attachment to its fruits (karmaṇy evādhikāras te). The chapter closes with the portrait of the sthita-prajña, the person of steady wisdom.

Chapter 3 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Karma-yoga (the Yoga of Action). No one can remain without acting even for a moment; so act, but as an offering (yajña), without selfish attachment. Kṛṣṇa explains the cycle of sacrifice that sustains the world, the example the wise must set for others (loka-saṅgraha), that one's own duty imperfectly done is better than another's done well, and that desire born of rajas is the enemy to be conquered.

Chapter 4 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Jñāna-karma-sannyāsa-yoga (the Yoga of Knowledge and the Renunciation of Action). Kṛṣṇa reveals that this yoga was taught of old to Vivasvān, and that He takes birth age after age to protect the good and establish dharma (yadā yadā hi dharmasya). He teaches seeing inaction in action, describes the many forms of sacrifice, and declares knowledge the supreme purifier, to be gained by reverence, inquiry and service to the wise.

Chapter 5 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Karma-sannyāsa-yoga (the Yoga of Renunciation). Arjuna asks which is better, renouncing action or performing it. Kṛṣṇa answers that both lead to the highest, but action without attachment is superior: the yogī works like a lotus leaf untouched by water, sees the same Self in a learned brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste, and finds the peace of Brahman within.

Chapter 6 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Ātma-saṁyama-yoga (the Yoga of Meditation). Lift yourself by yourself — the mind is both friend and enemy. Kṛṣṇa describes the practice of meditation: the seat, the posture, moderation in food and sleep, the mind steady as a lamp in a windless place. To Arjuna's doubt that the restless mind cannot be held, He answers: by practice and dispassion; and no one who does good ever comes to grief, even if the effort is left unfinished.

Chapter 7 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Jñāna-vijñāna-yoga (the Yoga of Knowledge and Realisation). Kṛṣṇa describes His lower nature (the eight elements of matter) and His higher nature (the life that sustains the world): all this is strung on Him like pearls on a thread. Four kinds of people worship Him — the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise; the wise one, who after many births knows that Vāsudeva is all, is very rare.

Chapter 8 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Akṣara-brahma-yoga (the Yoga of the Imperishable Brahman). Arjuna asks what Brahman, adhyātma, karma, adhibhūta and adhidaiva are. Kṛṣṇa explains them and teaches that whatever one remembers at the moment of death, to that one goes — so remember Him at all times and fight. He describes the cycles of the days and nights of Brahmā, and the two paths by which souls depart.

Chapter 9 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Rāja-vidyā-rāja-guhya-yoga (the Yoga of the Royal Knowledge and Royal Secret). The whole universe is pervaded by Kṛṣṇa's unmanifest form, yet He stands apart. Whatever is offered with love — a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water (patraṁ puṣpaṁ phalaṁ toyam) — He accepts; whoever worships Him with undivided devotion, He carries their burden. Even the gravest sinner who turns to Him is soon righteous: 'My devotee never perishes.'

Chapter 10 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Vibhūti-yoga (the Yoga of Divine Manifestations). Kṛṣṇa declares Himself the source of all, and Arjuna praises Him as the Supreme Brahman and asks to hear His glories. Kṛṣṇa lists His chief manifestations — among the Ādityas Viṣṇu, among lights the sun, among rivers the Gaṅgā, among the Pāṇḍavas Arjuna — and concludes that whatever is glorious, beautiful or mighty springs from a spark of His splendour.

Chapter 11 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Viśvarūpa-darśana-yoga (the Vision of the Cosmic Form). Granted divine sight, Arjuna beholds Kṛṣṇa's universal form — countless faces, eyes and arms, the radiance of a thousand suns — and sees the warriors of both armies rushing into His mouths. 'I am Time, the destroyer of worlds': Arjuna is to be merely the instrument. Terrified and awed, Arjuna praises Him and begs to see again the gentle four-armed and human form. Much of this chapter is in the Triṣṭubh metre.

Chapter 12 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Bhakti-yoga (the Yoga of Devotion). Arjuna asks who is better — those who worship the personal Lord or the unmanifest Imperishable. Kṛṣṇa answers that both reach Him, but the path of the unmanifest is harder for the embodied; He gives a ladder of practice for those who cannot fix their mind on Him at once, and closes with the beloved qualities of His devotee — without hatred, friendly and compassionate, the same in honour and dishonour.

Chapter 13 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Kṣetra-kṣetrajña-vibhāga-yoga (the Field and the Knower of the Field). The body is the field, and He who knows it is the knower of the field — and Kṛṣṇa is the knower in all fields. He lists the virtues that constitute knowledge, describes the Brahman that is to be known, and explains prakṛti and puruṣa: whoever sees the Lord dwelling equally in all beings, imperishable among the perishing, truly sees.

Chapter 14 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Guṇa-traya-vibhāga-yoga (the Three Guṇas). Kṛṣṇa explains how the three qualities of nature — sattva, rajas and tamas — bind the embodied soul: sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by attachment to action, tamas by delusion and sloth. Asked about the one who has transcended them, He describes the guṇātīta — equal in pleasure and pain, praise and blame — who serves Him with unwavering devotion.

Chapter 15 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Puruṣottama-yoga (the Supreme Person). The world is an eternal aśvattha tree with roots above and branches below, to be cut down with the axe of detachment. Kṛṣṇa is the light of the sun and moon, the digestive fire in all beings, seated in every heart; beyond the perishable and the imperishable, He is the Supreme Person, the Puruṣottama. This short chapter is traditionally recited before meals.

Chapter 16 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Daivāsura-sampad-vibhāga-yoga (the Divine and Demoniac Natures). Kṛṣṇa lists the divine qualities that lead to liberation — fearlessness, purity, charity, self-control, non-violence, truthfulness, compassion — and the demoniac ones that lead to bondage — hypocrisy, arrogance, anger and harshness. Lust, anger and greed are the three gates of hell; so let the scripture be your authority in deciding what to do.

Chapter 17 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Śraddhā-traya-vibhāga-yoga (the Three Kinds of Faith). Faith takes the form of one's nature: sāttvika, rājasa or tāmasa. Kṛṣṇa describes the three kinds of food, sacrifice, austerity (of body, speech and mind) and charity, and ends with the meaning of 'Om Tat Sat', the threefold designation of Brahman.

Chapter 18 of the Bhagavad Gītā, Mokṣa-sannyāsa-yoga (Liberation through Renunciation). Kṛṣṇa distinguishes renunciation (sannyāsa) from relinquishment (tyāga), analyses knowledge, action, doer, intellect, resolve and happiness by the three guṇas, and teaches that one attains perfection by worshipping Him through one's own duty. Then the final word: 'Abandon all dharmas and take refuge in Me alone; I will free you from all sins — do not grieve.' Arjuna's delusion is gone, and Sañjaya closes: where Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna are, there are fortune, victory and justice.

Seven verses on the greatness of the Gītā, traditionally chanted after the text: whoever reads this holy scripture with care attains the abode of Viṣṇu; a single bath in the waters of the Gītā washes away the dirt of saṁsāra; all the Upaniṣads are cows, the son of Nanda the milker, Arjuna the calf, and the Gītā the nectar-milk; one scripture, the song of Devakī's son; one God, Devakī's son; one mantra, His names; one duty, His service.

The Gītā-māhātmyam of the Varāha Purāṇa. After verses of meditation on Varāha, the boar incarnation who raised the earth on his tusk, the goddess Earth (Dharā) asks Lord Viṣṇu how unwavering devotion can arise in one still bound by prārabdha karma. Viṣṇu answers with the glories of the Gītā: its student is liberated and happy, untouched by sin like a lotus leaf by water; wherever the Gītā is read, all holy places are present; 'the Gītā is My supreme abode; relying on its knowledge I sustain the three worlds'; and He describes the merit of reciting the whole, half, a chapter, or even a single verse.

The Gītārtha-saṅgraha of Śrī Yāmunācārya (Āḷavandār), the great Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher: 32 verses summarising the meaning of the Bhagavad Gītā. It describes the Gītā's aim as Nārāyaṇa, attainable only through devotion arising from one's duty, knowledge and detachment; treats the three hexads of chapters (karma and jñāna yoga, bhakti yoga, and their synthesis); and gives the purport of each of the eighteen chapters in turn, ending with the four kinds of devotees and the glory of the jñānī.

The Gītā-māhātmyam of the Padma Purāṇa (Uttara-khaṇḍa, adhyāya 175) tells, for each chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā, a story of the power of reciting it. This is the story of the first chapter. Śiva tells Pārvatī how Viṣṇu Himself meditates on the Gītā, and narrates the story of Suśarman, a dissolute brāhmaṇa who died of a snakebite, passed through many hells, and was reborn as a bull, toiling for years under a cruel master. When the bull collapsed in the street, a courtesan gave him whatever merit she had, and he was freed and reborn a brāhmaṇa who remembered his past. Seeking her out, he learned the source of her merit: her pet parrot recited the first chapter of the Gītā every day. The parrot then told its own story — once a proud, envious scholar, reborn as a bird, it had learned the first chapter from sages in a hermitage before being caught by a fowler. Even one chapter, heard or recited, frees one from saṁsāra. (English translation: https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-bhagavad-gita-mahatmya/d/doc365756.html)

The Gītā-māhātmyam of the Padma Purāṇa (Uttara-khaṇḍa, adhyāya 176) tells, for each chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā, a story of the power of reciting it. This is the story of the second chapter. Kṛṣṇa tells Lakṣmī of Devaśarman, a learned and wealthy brāhmaṇa of Purandara who longed for liberation. A sage sent him to Mitravān, a goatherd of Saupura, whose forest home was so peaceful that tigers and goats lived side by side. Mitravān told him how a devoted worshipper of a Śivaliṅga in the forest had been given the second chapter of the Gītā, inscribed on a stone slab, by a visiting sage; wherever it was recited, enmity ceased — and that same chapter was the source of the peace of his own grove. Devaśarman returned home, learned the chapter properly, recited it daily, and reached the highest state. (English translation: https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-bhagavad-gita-mahatmya/d/doc365755.html)

The Gītā-māhātmyam of the Padma Purāṇa (Uttara-khaṇḍa, adhyāya 177) tells, for each chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā, a story of the power of reciting it. This is the story of the third chapter. The story of Jaḍa, a brāhmaṇa of Janasthāna who abandoned his duties for gambling, drink, hunting and adultery, and, when his wealth ran out, turned to theft. Killed by robbers on the road, he became a fierce, starving ghost. His devout son, travelling to Vārāṇasī to perform his father's rites, stopped at the very tree where Jaḍa had died and recited the third chapter of the Gītā. At once Jaḍa appeared in the sky, radiant, in a celestial chariot. He asked his son to recite the chapter for his brother and ancestors suffering in hell; the son did so, Viṣṇu's messengers ordered Yama to release them, and in time the son too reached Vaikuṇṭha. (English translation: https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-bhagavad-gita-mahatmya/d/doc365757.html)

The Gītā-māhātmyam of the Padma Purāṇa (Uttara-khaṇḍa, adhyāya 178) tells, for each chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā, a story of the power of reciting it. This is the story of the fourth chapter. The Lord tells Lakṣmī of Bharata, an ascetic of Vārāṇasī devoted to the fourth chapter of the Gītā. Two apsarases sent by Indra had once danced to disturb the penance of the sage Satyatapas on the Godāvarī; he cursed them to become badarī (jujube) trees, with release promised when Bharata, who remembered the fourth chapter, came to them. Bharata rested between the two trees while on pilgrimage, and they were freed — reborn as girls who remembered their past. They later found him again, thanked him for freeing them both from the curse and from worldly existence, took up the fourth chapter themselves, and attained the highest state. (English translation: https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-bhagavad-gita-mahatmya/d/doc365758.html)

The Gītā-māhātmyam of the Padma Purāṇa (Uttara-khaṇḍa, adhyāya 179) tells, for each chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā, a story of the power of reciting it. This is the story of the fifth chapter. The story of Piṅgala, a brāhmaṇa of the Bhadra country who gave up Vedic study for music and dance, became a favourite at court, seduced other men's wives and slandered the good; and of his wife Aruṇā, who killed him and hid his body. He was reborn a vulture and she a female parrot, and they tormented each other until both died — the parrot drowning in water held in a human skull. Brought before Yama, they asked why they were bound for heaven despite their deeds. Yama explained: the skull belonged to a brāhmaṇa named Baṭu who had lived on the banks of the Gaṅgā reciting the fifth chapter of the Gītā daily; touching his remains had purified them. They rose in a celestial chariot to Viṣṇu's abode. (English translation: https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-bhagavad-gita-mahatmya/d/doc365759.html)

The Gītā-māhātmyam of the Padma Purāṇa (Uttara-khaṇḍa, adhyāya 180) tells, for each chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā, a story of the power of reciting it. This is the story of the sixth chapter. Divine swans flying over Pratiṣṭhāna on the Godāvarī praise King Jñānaśruti's glory, but say that the sage Raikya shines brighter still. The king sends his charioteer across the holy places of India — Vārāṇasī, Gayā, Kedāra, Dvārakā and more — until he finds Raikya in Kashmir, sitting under a cart, scratching himself. Jñānaśruti comes with a cart, mules, a necklace and a thousand cows; Raikya angrily sends him away as a 'śūdra'. Humbled, the king falls at his feet and asks the secret of his radiance. Raikya replies: 'I recite the sixth chapter of the Gītā every day.' Learning it, the king was freed, and even the gods who watched were amazed. (The story echoes that of Raikva and Jānaśruti in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.) (English translation: https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-bhagavad-gita-mahatmya/d/doc365760.html)

The Gītā-māhātmyam of the Padma Purāṇa (Uttara-khaṇḍa, adhyāya 181) tells, for each chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā, a story of the power of reciting it. This is the story of the seventh chapter. The story of Śaṅkukarṇa, a brāhmaṇa of Pāṭaliputra who lived by trade, amassed wealth, and neglected dharma. Killed by a snakebite during a family celebration, he was reborn as a serpent guarding his buried treasure. He appeared in his sons' dreams; one longed for his release, another only for the treasure. When the greedy son came to dig up the anthill, the serpent spoke and told him that only the seventh chapter of the Gītā could free him: at his śrāddha they must feed a brāhmaṇa who recites it. The sons did so; Śaṅkukarṇa cast off the serpent form, took a divine body, and gave them the treasure, which they spent on charitable works; reciting the seventh chapter, they too were liberated.
